sheet.howExamined: M7, Paper 1 (no calculator) and Paper 2 (calculator), 50 marks in 75 minutes each. About one question a series, usually on Paper 2 and in the second half of the paper, worth 4 marks in two parts. Part (a) is the tree, 2 or 3 marks, with a mark for the branch probabilities and a mark for the outcome labels (Summer 2025 M7 Paper 2 Q12; November 2025 M7 Paper 2 Q14; Summer 2023 M7 Paper 2 Q16). Part (b) reads one probability off it, 1 or 2 marks, and is where the multiplying is tested. Paper 1 versions demand the fraction arithmetic by hand, and some questions build the tree from two groups rather than one bag (November 2024 M7 Paper 1 Q14).

Changing the probabilities on the second set of branches although the item was replaced (November 2025 M7 Paper 2 Q14)
Putting one stage's probabilities on the other stage's branches (Summer 2025 M7 Paper 2 Q12)
Writing a pair of branches that does not add to 1 (Summer 2025 M7 Paper 2 Q12)

steps.decision: There are 8 counters, so each probability is a count out of 8. Writing both down, even the one you may not need, keeps the pair adding to 1.

steps.working: Second pick: the counter went back, so $P(\text{yellow}) = \tfrac{3}{8}$ and $P(\text{purple}) = \tfrac{5}{8}$ again.
steps.decision: With replacement the bag is unchanged, so the second pair of branches repeats the first. Nothing about the first colour matters.

options: Because the counter was put back, so the bag is the same as before
Because the two colours are equally likely
Because a tree diagram always has the same numbers twice
whyMenu.explain: The counter is replaced, so there are still 3 yellow among 8. Had it been kept, the second-stage numbers would have to change.

steps.decision: Along a branch you multiply, because both picks have to go that way. Adding would give $\tfrac{3}{4}$, which is larger than one yellow on its own and cannot be right.

steps.working: One of each happens two ways: yellow then purple, $\tfrac{15}{64}$, and purple then yellow, $\tfrac{15}{64}$.
steps.decision: The question does not say which colour comes first, so both paths fit. Missing the second path halves the answer.
Across branches you add, because either path will do. Check: the four paths $\tfrac{9}{64}$, $\tfrac{15}{64}$, $\tfrac{15}{64}$ and $\tfrac{25}{64}$ add to 1.

steps.working: $P(\text{in}) = 0.7$, so $P(\text{not in}) = 1 - 0.7 = 0.3$, on both pairs of branches.
steps.decision: Each pair of branches has to add to 1, and the serves are independent, so the second pair repeats the first.
Along the top branch both serves go in, so the probabilities multiply. Adding would give $1.4$, which is greater than 1 and could not be a probability.
At least one covers three of the four paths, so go the short way: work out the one path that has no serve in at all.
Subtract from 1, never from anything else. Check: both in, neither in and exactly one in are $0.49$, $0.09$ and $0.42$, which add to 1.

items.skill: Read a single probability off a collection
items.stem: A bag holds 3 yellow and 5 purple counters. One counter is drawn without looking. What is the probability that it is yellow?

options.feedback: 3 of the 8 counters are yellow, so the probability is $\tfrac{3}{8}$.
That compares yellow with purple rather than with the whole bag. A probability is out of the total.
The value is right but a probability is written as a fraction, a decimal or a percentage, never as a ratio.
That is the purple counters. The question asks for yellow.

items.stem: Work out $\tfrac{3}{8} \times \tfrac{2}{5}$, giving a fraction in its simplest form.

options.feedback: Multiply the numerators and multiply the denominators: $\tfrac{3}{8} \times \tfrac{2}{5} = \tfrac{3}{20}$.
That is the two fractions added, not multiplied.
The numerators have been added and the first denominator kept, which is neither operation.
The numerators have been multiplied but the denominator left alone. Both parts of the fraction multiply.

items.skill: Find the probability that an event does not happen
items.stem: The probability that a serve goes in is $0.7$. What is the probability that it does not go in?

options.feedback: $1 - 0.7 = 0.3$. In and not in are the only outcomes, so they add to 1.
That is the probability that it does go in.
That is more than 1, which no probability can be.
Two outcomes does not make them equally likely; the given probability tells you the split.

items.skill: Keep the second-stage probabilities unchanged when the item is replaced
items.stem: A bag holds 3 yellow and 5 purple counters. One is taken, its colour noted, and put back. What probability goes on the yellow branch of the second pick?

options.feedback: The counter went back, so the bag is unchanged: still 3 yellow among 8.
That is the probability after a yellow counter has been kept out. Here it was replaced, so nothing changes.
The denominator has been reduced as if a counter were missing. The counter is back in the bag.
That is the purple branch. The two branches of a pair carry different probabilities, and they add to 1.

items.stem: From the same bag with replacement, what is the probability of purple on both picks?

options.feedback: $\tfrac{5}{8} \times \tfrac{5}{8} = \tfrac{25}{64}$. Along a branch, multiply.
That adds along the branch. Both picks have to be purple, which makes the outcome rarer, so the probabilities multiply.
The second branch has been changed as if the counter were kept. It was replaced, so the second probability is the same as the first.
That is one pick only. A path through two stages has two probabilities on it.

items.skill: Add the paths that fit the description
items.stem: From the same bag with replacement, what is the probability of one yellow and one purple, in either order?

options.feedback: Yellow then purple is $\tfrac{15}{64}$ and purple then yellow is $\tfrac{15}{64}$, and both fit, so they add to $\tfrac{15}{32}$.
That is one path only. Purple first then yellow is also one of each colour.
The two paths have been multiplied together. Either path will do, so they add.
That adds the two branch probabilities from one stage, which always gives 1.

items.skill: Answer an at-least-one question through the complement
items.stem: From the same bag with replacement, what is the probability of at least one yellow in the two picks?

options.feedback: The only path with no yellow is purple then purple, $\tfrac{25}{64}$, so the answer is $1 - \tfrac{25}{64} = \tfrac{39}{64}$.
That is the probability of no yellow at all. At least one is what is left when that is taken from 1.
That is exactly one yellow. At least one also includes both being yellow.
That is both counters yellow, which is only one of the three paths that contain a yellow.

items.skill: Know what a branch must carry and what a pair must add to
items.stem: A tree diagram has been drawn for two stages. Which of these means a mark will be lost even when the arithmetic is right?

options.text: A pair of branches with no outcome written beside them
options.feedback: Every branch needs its outcome label as well as its probability; the reports name missing labels as the commonest lost mark on these questions.

options.text: A pair of branches carrying probabilities that add to 1
options.feedback: That is exactly what a pair should do, so nothing is lost.

options.text: The same probabilities written on both sets of branches
options.feedback: With replacement that is right: the second stage repeats the first.

options.text: A pair of branches carrying $0.3$ and $0.6$
options.feedback: Those do not add to 1, so one of them is out; but the fault the reports name most is the missing label.

parts.stem:
A bag holds 3 yellow and 5 purple counters. One counter is taken, its colour noted, and put back. A second counter is then taken.

The tree diagram has been started for you, with the branches labelled but no probabilities written on.

Write down the probability that goes on the purple branch of the second pick.

parts.stem:

Give your answer as a fraction in its simplest form.

scheme.for: both paths considered, so two products added

hints: Yellow then purple and purple then yellow are different paths.
Work out one path, then account for the other.
parts.workedSolution: Yellow then purple is $\tfrac{3}{8} \times \tfrac{5}{8} = \tfrac{15}{64}$ and purple then yellow is $\tfrac{5}{8} \times \tfrac{3}{8} = \tfrac{15}{64}$. Both paths are one of each colour, so they add: $\tfrac{15}{64} + \tfrac{15}{64} = \tfrac{15}{32}$.

commonErrors.feedback: That is one path only, and the multiplying marks stand. Purple first then yellow is also one of each, so the second product is added.
The two paths have been multiplied together. Along a path you multiply; across paths either will do, so they add.

parts.stem:
From the same bag of 3 yellow and 5 purple counters, with the first counter replaced before the second is taken:

Work out the probability that at least one of the two counters is yellow.

Give your answer as a fraction.

scheme.for: 5/8 x 5/8 = 25/64 seen as the no-yellow path

hints: Three of the four paths have a yellow in them, so find the one that does not.
Subtract that path's probability from 1.
parts.workedSolution: The only path with no yellow is purple then purple, $\tfrac{5}{8} \times \tfrac{5}{8} = \tfrac{25}{64}$. So $P(\text{at least one yellow}) = 1 - \tfrac{25}{64} = \tfrac{39}{64}$.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the probability of no yellow at all, which earns the first method mark. At least one is what is left when it is taken from 1.
That is exactly one yellow, from the two mixed paths. At least one also includes both counters being yellow.

parts.stem:
A spinner has 4 equal sections, 1 of them blue.

The spinner is spun three times.

Work out the probability that it never lands on blue.

Give your answer as a fraction.
hints: Three spins means three factors along the path.
Each spin is independent, so the probability stays the same.
parts.workedSolution: $P(\text{not blue}) = \tfrac{3}{4}$ on every spin, and the spins are independent, so $P(\text{never blue}) = \tfrac{3}{4} \times \tfrac{3}{4} \times \tfrac{3}{4} = \tfrac{27}{64}$.

commonErrors.feedback: That is two spins. Three spins means three factors along the path, so multiply by $\tfrac{3}{4}$ once more.
Adding the three probabilities gives a number above 1, which no probability can be. Along a path, multiply.

parts.stem:
On one journey a driver passes two traffic lights. The probability that a light is green as she reaches it is $0.4$, and the two lights work independently.

Work out the probability that both lights are green.
hints: Follow the top path of the tree.
Along a path, multiply.

commonErrors.feedback: That adds along the path. Both lights have to be green, which is rarer than one, so the probabilities multiply.
That is one light only. The path through the tree carries two probabilities.

parts.stem: Work out the probability that exactly one of the two lights is green.

scheme.for: 0.4 x 0.6 seen, with both paths considered

hints: Green then not green, and not green then green, are different paths.
Work out one path, then add the other.
parts.workedSolution: Green then not green is $0.4 \times 0.6 = 0.24$, and not green then green is the same. Both paths have exactly one green, so $P = 0.24 + 0.24 = 0.48$.

commonErrors.feedback: That is one path only, and the multiplying mark stands. The other light could be the green one, so the second path is added.
That takes both-green away from 1, which leaves everything else, including neither being green. Exactly one is two paths, added.

parts.stem:
A spinner has 4 equal sections, 1 of them blue. It is spun, and then spun again.

Work out the probability that it lands on blue both times.

Give your answer as a fraction.
hints: The spinner is unchanged between spins.
Along a path, multiply.

commonErrors.feedback: That adds along the path. Landing on blue twice is rarer than landing on blue once, so the probabilities multiply.
The second branch has been changed as if a section were used up. A spinner is not a bag: every spin starts from the same 4 sections.

parts.stem:
Work out the probability that the spinner lands on blue at least once in the two spins.

Give your answer as a fraction.
hints: Find the one path with no blue at all.
Take it away from 1.
parts.workedSolution: The only path with no blue is not blue, then not blue: $\tfrac{3}{4} \times \tfrac{3}{4} = \tfrac{9}{16}$. So $P(\text{at least one blue}) = 1 - \tfrac{9}{16} = \tfrac{7}{16}$.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the probability of no blue at all, which earns the method mark. At least one is what is left after taking it from 1.
That takes blue-twice away from 1. The opposite of at least one blue is no blue, not two blues.

findTheMistake.stem: Ruairí was asked: a bag holds 3 yellow and 5 purple counters, and one is taken, noted and put back before a second is taken. Work out the probability that both are yellow. His working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 1 is right: the counter goes back, so both picks carry $\tfrac{3}{8}$. Line 2 adds them. Along a branch both picks have to go the same way, which is a multiplication: $\tfrac{3}{8} \times \tfrac{3}{8} = \tfrac{9}{64}$.
findTheMistake.feedback: The size of the answer is the warning: $\tfrac{3}{4}$ is larger than the chance of a single yellow, and demanding two yellows cannot make the outcome more likely. Along a branch, multiply.

prompts.prompt: What do you do with the probabilities along one branch of a tree?
prompts.answer: Multiply along a branch, because every stage on that path has to happen.

prompts.prompt: What do you do with two branches that both fit the description asked for?
prompts.answer: Add the two branches, because either path will do.

prompts.prompt: An item is taken and put back before the second pick. What happens to the second set of branches?
prompts.answer: Nothing changes: the bag is the same, so the second stage carries the same probabilities as the first.

prompts.prompt: What must every branch of a tree diagram carry, and what must each pair add to?
prompts.answer: An outcome label and a probability, and each pair of branches leaving one point adds to 1.

prompts.prompt: How do you answer an at-least-one question from a tree?
prompts.answer: Work out the probability of none, then subtract it from 1.

prompts.prompt: How can a completed two-stage tree check itself?
prompts.answer: The four path probabilities add to 1, and no probability on it is greater than 1.

prompts.prompt: A question asks for one of each, in either order. What do you do?
prompts.answer: Multiply along each order, then add the two orders together.

prompts.prompt: A tree is built from two groups of different sizes. What goes on a branch?
prompts.answer: A probability out of that group's own total, not the number of people in the group.

findings.asked: Complete a two-stage tree from two given probabilities, then read one probability off it.
findings.wentWrong: Probabilities were placed on the wrong set of branches, labels were left off, and a pair of branches was written that did not add to 1. In the second part a very common answer was the sum of two branch probabilities rather than their product.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Labelled both stages before writing any number, then multiplied along the path.
findings.rule: Label every branch with its outcome and its probability, and multiply along the path.

findings.asked: Complete a tree for two rolls of a biased dice, then find the probability of no sixes.
findings.wentWrong: Many completed the tree for two marks, but a mark was lost wherever the outcome labels were missing. Some changed the fractions on the second set of branches although nothing about the dice had changed. In the second part, only a few reached the product, and some added the fractions without noticing that the result was greater than 1.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Kept the second stage identical to the first and multiplied the two fractions.
findings.rule: Independent events keep the same probabilities on the second set of branches.

findings.asked: Complete a tree for two days of weather, then find a combined probability.
findings.wentWrong: The diagrams were a decent attempt, but the outcome labels were often forgotten. In the second part many did not know to multiply and added the branch probabilities instead.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Wrote both outcomes on every branch, then multiplied along the path they needed.

findings.asked: Build a tree from two groups of different sizes, then find a probability from it.
findings.wentWrong: Some branch ends carried raw counts instead of fractions, labels were missing, and the overall total was used where each group's own total was needed. Only a small minority finished the second part, and some added the two fractions rather than multiplying.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Turned each count into a probability out of its own group before drawing anything.
findings.rule: Each branch carries a probability out of its own group's total.

findings.asked: The probability that two independent events combine in a described way.
findings.wentWrong: Many added instead of multiplying. Of those who multiplied, some counted only two of the four ordered outcomes that fitted the description.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Listed every ordered outcome that fitted, multiplied along each, then added across.
findings.rule: List every order that fits, multiply along each, then add.

insight.ruleToRemember: Label every branch with its outcome and its probability; with replacement the second stage repeats the first; multiply along a path, add the paths that fit; at least one is 1 minus none; the four paths add to 1.
insight.aStarSignal: Reaching an at-least-one answer through 1 minus the probability of none without being prompted, on a fully labelled tree.
